question_text: A 59-year-old woman is admitted to the intensive care unit after surgery following a motor vehicle collision. She has received a total of four units of packed red blood cells. Physical examination shows dry mucous membranes and flat neck veins. Serum studies show a creatinine of 2.1 mg/dL and urine microscopy shows granular, muddy-brown casts. A renal biopsy specimen is obtained and examined under light microscopy. Which of the following reversible cellular changes is most likely to be present?

                    ### Question
                    A 59-year-old woman is admitted to the intensive care unit after surgery following a motor vehicle collision. She has received a total of four units of packed red blood cells. Physical examination shows dry mucous membranes and flat neck veins. Serum studies show a creatinine of 2.1 mg/dL and urine microscopy shows granular, muddy-brown casts. A renal biopsy specimen is obtained and examined under light microscopy. Which of the following reversible cellular changes is most likely to be present?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Vacuolization of the endoplasmatic reticulum
opb. Rupture of lysosomes
opc. Swelling of the mitochondria
opd. Release of cytochrome C
ope. Protease-induced cytoskeletal damage

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The 59-year-old woman post-surgery shows signs of acute kidney injury, indicated by elevated creatinine levels and granular, muddy-brown casts in urine microscopy, consistent with acute tubular necrosis (ATN). In ATN, reversible cellular changes are expected, primarily characterized by cellular swelling. The most likely cellular change present is swelling of the mitochondria, which aligns with the consensus on the pathophysiology of acute tubular injury. Other options, such as vacuolization of the endoplasmic reticulum or rupture of lysosomes, are less specific to the acute tubular injury context. Therefore, the best-supported option is 'swelling of the mitochondria.'
